items.title: What time is F1's 2026 Singapore Grand Prix? Full weekend schedule
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Formula 1 switches back to its sprint race format and has its first night race of 2026 this weekend as it arrives at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The twisty street track often throws up curveballs and leaves regular pacesetters struggling - and this time it comes straight after the shock of Red Bull's emphatic defeat of Mercedes in Malaysia.

Will that prove to be the start of a new late-season trend, or will Mercedes swiftly regain its superiority? We'll find out at the Marina Bay track this weekend.

Below you'll find the all-important session times for the weekend, as well as all the information on where to watch the action on Apple TV.

items.title: Russell at risk of 'double whammy' grid penalty
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
George Russell could face a further “double whammy” hit following his Malaysia retirement if his Mercedes Formula 1 power unit cannot be fixed.

The Mercedes driver had looked on course to take a podium finish at Sepang before he was forced to stop his car five laps from the chequered flag with a suspected engine problem.

The stoppage was a big blow to his already slim world championship hopes, as it meant the gap between himself and team-mate Kimi Antonelli has opened up to 84 points with just seven races remaining.

But worse than the setback in the standings is that the failure could further hurt his chances of beating Antonelli in the next races.

Russell is on the edge in terms of mileage with his current pool of engines, and he had been holding out for a switch to a fresh version until an expected upgraded Mercedes specification appears at the United States Grand Prix.

Mercedes is set to make use of opportunities under F1’s ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules to bring a new power unit homologation to Austin for all its cars.

items.title: Japanese Grand Prix 2026 MotoGP rider rankings
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The two main MotoGP title contenders separated themselves from the field again in the Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi - but does Marc Marquez's 37-pointer warrant P1 in the rankings, or is there another candidate?

2nd 1st 1st

One of the easier P1 selections this year (and Marquez's fourth this season, for reference).

The Ducati didn't have the clear edge over the Aprilia at Motegi some may have expected - but Marquez did have a clear edge over everyone else.

Friday to Saturday to Sunday, he was simply too strong - too in tune with the various twists of the weekend with the new surface and revised allocation, too comfortable running at consistent top pace, too precise in turning P2 into P1 in both races.

1st 3rd 2nd

Championship-spec Jorge Martin is turning up here, though Marquez has shown that won't necessarily be enough.

But Friday had promised a much more damaging weekend for Martin - who needed Pedro Acosta's help to ensure a Q2 spot - and yet he turned it around completely with an "unbelievable" overnight improvement.

Excessive tyre spin cost him on Saturday - he was maybe unlucky (and maybe careless) to touch the green paint on the final lap, but was anyway lucky that other strong riders had been taken out.

items.title: Key figure in Honda's F1 return to be replaced in 2027
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda will get a new racing boss next year after the retirement of current president and CEO Koji Watanabe, who helped manage the manufacturer’s official return to Formula 1.

Watanabe will be replaced as the head of Honda Racing Corporation by Keiichi Yasuda on January 1, slightly earlier than executive-level changes would typically happen in April to align with the motorsport season.

Yasuda is currently HRC’s executive vice president and representative director.

Like Watanabe, he is a company man who has been with Honda since 1990. Prior to his HRC leadership role, which included overseeing Honda’s official F1 return under the new 2026 engine regulations, Watanabe rose to be a senior figure on the communications and marketing side within Honda.

He assumed the HRC job as part of Honda’s restructuring of its motorsport efforts in 2022 when it unified its motorcycle and car racing programmes under the same entity.

That made Watanabe a senior figure and spokesperson for Honda’s enduring relationship with Red Bull to the end of 2025 and then its new engine project with Aston Martin this year.

items.title: Mercedes to run old + new car spec in Singapore amid upgrade doubts
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is to run a back-to-back comparison between its new and old Formula 1 aero packages in Singapore to better understand whether or not its latest upgrade has worked.

The manufacturer had arrived at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia hopeful that a new development step for its W17 would lift it clear at the front of F1.

However, the expected 0.3-second improvement did not materialise, and team principal Toto Wolff reckoned it had instead dropped its performance by up to half a second.

That left the door open for Red Bull's Max Verstappen to take his first pole position and victory of the season for Red Bull.

The surprise lack of pace from Mercedes prompted some deep post-race analysis to understand what went wrong, and whether what played out was entirely down to the aero package or was linked to the rough track surface.

items.title: F1's cost cap fix: What's actually proposed, and for when
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 teams are set to discuss a potential overhaul of financial regulations for 2027 aimed at ending what has been labelled a “cost cap trap” for smaller squads.

The Race has learned that the idea of a catch-up mechanism being added to the cost cap is set to be raised at the next meeting of the F1 Commission, which takes place in November.

The plan is being pushed for by Williams boss James Vowles, who wants revised cost cap rules in place for the start of next season to avoid what he thinks has become a “two-tiered” F1, where the big four teams have pulled away from the chasing pack.

Vowles sees this situation as a consequence of legacy advantages having been locked in.

Vowles fears that the more this becomes bedded in, then the bigger the risk that the divide becomes permanent.

Should teams not have the chance to mix it with those at the front, they will become less attractive for sponsors and there will be less incentive to invest. That will stop progress, lead to even worse results and see team valuations go down.

Williams is not calling for an end to the cost cap, which it thinks has been hugely positive in bringing financial stability to F1 and adding value to all the current teams because there is no longer an arms race of spending.

items.title: The 'weird' car theory sparked by F1 pecking order surprises
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Among the factors potentially behind a swing in Formula 1's recent pecking order in Malaysia is how an extreme track surface could have made some cars behave in a "weird way" aerodynamically. 

Mercedes and McLaren had claimed 14 of 15 pole positions between them prior to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and won 13 of the 15 races in 2026 so far. 

But they were comprehensively bested by Red Bull, and outqualified by Ferrari too, as Max Verstappen took advantage of F1's return to Sepang and its unique challenge to best the usual benchmarks. Even Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies admitted this was a "surprise". 

A prominent theme of the week was how the Sepang surface was unusually rough, ironically only matched by Bahrain's own Sakhir circuit, which this grand prix replaced. Mekies said the extreme heat, track roughness and layout of the track meant "most of the cars out there were out of their ideal operating window". 

An open, abrasive track surface combined with high temperatures is an established and well understood challenge, though. More interesting was a more intricate variable that hints at how that kind of surface disturbs a car's aerodynamic performance.

items.title: Aleix Espargaro back to MotoGP in latest Honda shuffle
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
Honda test rider Aleix Espargaro will return to MotoGP action at this weekend’s Indonesian Grand Prix, replacing fellow test rider Taka Nakagami as stand-in for the unwell Joan Mir.

Espargaro has been drafted in because Nakagami crashed out on his very first lap of the weekend last time out at Motegi and broke his collarbone.

Espargaro’s return to action doesn’t just mark his first time racing since last year’s season finale at Valencia, but it's one of the few times he'll ride a MotoGP machine since a private test crash at Sepang in April left the three-time race winner with a career-threatening shattered back.

He fell during a private outing alongside Nakagami at the Malaysian circuit earlier this year, breaking four vertebrae and needing to be medically evacuated back to Spain before requiring multiple surgeries to stabilise the fractures. 

“It is always a great honour to join the factory Honda team in MotoGP,” said Espargaro in a team statement. "I want to say thank you to them for trusting me to ride while Joan and Taka recover.

items.title: The action Mercedes can take over confusing F1 upgrade
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Mercedes is keeping all options on the table, including running a potential back-to-back test with its old package in Singapore, to try to understand why its latest Formula 1 upgrade did not deliver the step forward hoped for.

However, rather than unleashing a predicted 0.3-second gain in laptime, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff wondered if it had actually resulted in a step back of up to 0.5 seconds as rival Red Bull took its first victory of the season with Max Verstappen.

Mercedes was at a loss to explain why improvements being shown on the data in terms of extra downforce were not manifesting themselves in the laptimes.

And it was particularly perplexed about why the gains it had made in high-speed corners had come at the cost of low-speed performance, and had appeared to impact its straightline speed as well.

The key answer Mercedes needs from what happened in Malaysia is how much of its performance deficit was down to the new package and how much of it was down to the unique circumstances of the Sepang event - with high temperatures and a rough track surface.

items.title: Eight things we learned from F1's Malaysia weekend
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
From another Red Bull milestone to multiple teams being confused about why they were struggling, to a new flaw in the 2026 regulations being exposed, Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia taught us plenty.

Here's everything we learned from the first F1 weekend at Sepang in nine years...

F1's wet-weather problem is only getting worse

F1 has long looked allergic to racing in the rain over the last decade and the 2026 regulations seem to have made that allergy even worse.

The exact "software bug" that sent things haywire at Sepang wasn't a specific allergy to rain - the cars didn't break down directly because of the water on track. But it was the uniquely low-speed conditions created by the wet Sepang circuit that exposed the bug in the electronic control units fitted to the cars.

And it came after some already glum predictions of how the 2026 F1 cars would cope with a rain-soaked track. Isack Hadjar, who tested at a wet Suzuka earlier this year, said: "The only thing I remember from Japan is that the tyres have zero grip. It would make the racing very dangerous with a lot of water".

items.title: Podcast: Should F1 have avoided its Malaysia farce?
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
On the latest episode of The Race F1 Podcast, Edd Straw is joined by Jon Noble and Scott Mitchell-Malm to discuss the Malaysia-hosted Bahrain Grand Prix.

It was a race that'll be remembered for Max Verstappen taking his and Red Bull’s first victory of 2026, but it was also one marred by chaos at the first attempt to start it. So what caused the farcical scenes that played out?

That's the key question tackled in part one of the podcast, before Edd, Jon and Scott explain Verstappen and Red Bull's supreme - and somewhat shock - pace this weekend, ask whether Ferrari's tyre blunder cost Lewis Hamilton a shot at victory, and unpack all of the race's other big talking points.
